clinical_knowledge.topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (median nerve compression), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cervical radiculopathy (C6/C7) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Thenar muscle atrophy.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Entrapment of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel causing nocturnal numbness and tingling in the radial three and a half digits.

must_ask.say: Are the numbness and burning located in your thumb, index, and middle fingers?
Does the hand numbness wake you up at night needing to shake your hands for relief?
Do you drop objects frequently or struggle to open jars or button shirts?
Do you perform repetitive wrist flexing activities or heavy computer typing?
Does holding your wrists bent together worsen the tingling within a minute?

history.answer: My right hand has been burning and tingling, especially my thumb and index finger, and it gets a lot worse at night.
It feels like a burning numbness and pins and needles, and my fingers feel a bit stiff and clumsy rather than paralyzed.
The tingling is in my right thumb, index, and middle finger, plus the side of my ring finger. My pinky finger and my left hand feel completely fine.
It started gradually about three months ago without any specific injury, and it has been steadily progressing since then.
At first it only happened after long typing sessions, but lately it is happening every single day and waking me from sleep.
I can still use my hand, but fastening small buttons feels clumsy and opening jar lids has become difficult.
Yes, I wake up two or three times a week in the middle of the night because my hand is burning and numb.
Vigorously shaking my hand or dangling it off the side of the mattress helps bring the feeling back.
Typing continuously at my computer or holding my wrist bent downward for a while triggers the burning sensation.
No, I do not have any neck pain, shoulder pain, or shooting pains traveling down my arm.
No, I haven't had slurred speech, facial drooping, vision changes, or dizziness.
No problems with controlling my bladder or bowels, and no numbness around my groin area.
No, I have no trouble breathing, swallowing, or chewing, and my eyelids are not drooping.
I have not noticed any twitching muscles or visible shrinking in the fleshy pad of my thumb.
No, I haven't had any stomach bug, diarrhea, or feverish cold recently.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart problems.
I eat meat regularly, have never had stomach surgery, and only have a glass of beer on rare occasions.
No, I have never taken steroids, water pills, or cancer medications.
I work full-time as a data entry clerk typing on a keyboard all day, but I do not rest on my elbows or squat.
I suspect this might be wrist strain from long hours at the computer, or possibly a pinched nerve in my wrist.
I am really worried that I might lose strength in my right hand and won't be able to do my work anymore.
I am hoping to get a wrist splint to wear at night, and I want to see if I need a nerve conduction test.
I have an underactive thyroid, which was diagnosed three years ago and has been stable on medication.
I have never had any surgeries and have never stayed in a hospital.
I take Levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily in the morning, and I do not take any over-the-counter painkillers or vitamins.
I have no allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I am a non-smoker and have never smoked.
I only drink an occasional beer maybe once or twice a month, and nothing more.
I work as an office clerk doing data entry, and I live with my wife and son in an apartment.
There is no history of nerve disorders, stroke, or muscle diseases in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Phalen test and Tinel sign over the right volar wrist reproduce numbness and tingling in the thumb and index finger; wrist and hand joints show full active range of motion without swelling or warmth.
Reduced pinprick and light touch sensation over the palmar aspect of the right thumb, index, and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the hypothenar eminence and dorsal hand.
Motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally in all upper extremity muscle groups except for mild weakness (4+/5) on resisted right thumb abduction; thenar bulk is preserved without atrophy.
Biceps, brachioradialis, and triceps deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally, and Hoffman and Babinski signs are absent.
Cervical spine has full range of motion without midline tenderness, and Spurling test is negative bilaterally.
Facial symmetry is intact, speech is fluent, extraocular movements are full without ptosis, and palate elevates symmetrically.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and moves smoothly on swallowing without palpable nodules or bruits.
